summary: Defines a protocol for generating Link-Quality-Reports on PPP links, letting each end learn how well the link is performing. It is on the standards track as a draft standard.

eli5.summary: Two computers talking on a line check how many of their messages are getting through, like counting how many letters arrived.

questions: what is ppp link quality monitoring
how does ppp measure link quality
what is a link quality report
what is the lqr reporting period
subtitle: How the two ends of a PPP link count packets and octets and swap reports to see how well the link is doing.

tldr.problem: Links drop or corrupt data, and a PPP endpoint may want to know when and how often, for example to switch to another route or link.
tldr.mechanism: Each end keeps counters of packets and octets sent and received and periodically sends them to its peer in a Link-Quality-Report (LQR). Comparing successive reports shows the loss in each direction.
tldr.outcome: PPP specifies the mechanism but leaves the policy, how to judge quality and what to do about it, to each implementation. The RFC is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1333.

today: RFC 1989 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 1333. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Monitor a PPP Link
sections.content:
Each end of a PPP link first sends LCP packets to configure the link during the Link Establishment phase. During the Authentication and Network-Layer Protocol phases the link may be tested to see whether its quality is sufficient. This testing is completely optional.

If an implementation wants the peer to use a specific link quality monitoring protocol, it MUST negotiate it with the Quality-Protocol Configuration Option during Link Establishment. Negotiation is independent in each direction, but a peer that agrees to send Quality-Protocol packets MUST process them correctly on reception, even if it does not request them or implement a monitoring policy.

The motivation is simple: packets can be dropped or corrupted by line noise, equipment failure or buffer overruns. Knowing when and how often lets a router prefer another route or an implementation switch to an alternate link.
sections.eli5: Wires sometimes lose messages. This system lets each side check how many are getting lost, if they want to.

sections.title: Mechanism Versus Policy
sections.content:
The RFC splits link quality monitoring into a mechanism and a policy. PPP fully specifies the mechanism: the Link-Quality-Report packet and the procedure for using it. PPP does not specify a policy, meaning how to judge link quality or what to do when it is inadequate. That is an implementation decision and can differ at each end. Implementations are encouraged to experiment, and the fixed mechanism ensures that two implementations with different policies still interoperate.

To allow flexible policies, data loss is measured in packets, octets and Link-Quality-Reports. Each half of the link, inbound and outbound, is measured separately, and all measurements are sent to both ends so each side can judge both directions. The mechanism is also meant to suit multi-process implementations with hardware support, so the packet format and the reference points for counting are defined carefully.
sections.eli5: Everyone agrees on how to count and how to report the counts. What to do about a bad count is up to each side.

sections.title: Counters and Logical Processes
sections.content:
Each side counts packets and octets transmitted and successfully received, and sends them to its peer. The counters only ever increase, like sequence numbers. By subtracting the values in successive reports, a receiver computes a delta and compares the numbers to judge quality. Relative numbers are sent because they greatly simplify link synchronization.

The report uses the SNMP MIB-II interface counters, plus three 32-bit counters:

  • OutLQRs increases by one for each transmitted LQR.
  • InLQRs increases by one for each received LQR.
  • InGoodOctets counts octets of successfully received packets, leaving out frames counted in ifInDiscards and ifInErrors.

All octets included in the FCS calculation MUST be counted, along with the FCS octets and one flag octet per frame. Other flag sequences and escape bits or octets MUST NOT be counted. Counts inserted in an LQR MUST include the LQR itself.

The mechanism is described with five logical processes at each end: Link-Manager, Mux, Tx, Rx and Demux. The Link-Manager sends and receives LQRs and implements the policy. Mux gives LQRs the highest possible priority. Tx counts outgoing data and MUST follow Mux. Rx counts incoming data and Demux MUST follow it.
sections.eli5: Each side keeps running tallies of messages sent and messages received, which only go up. Comparing two tallies from different times shows how many were lost in between.

sections.title: The Quality-Protocol Option
sections.content:
Implementations MUST be prepared to receive the Quality-Protocol Configuration Option for the LQR, but negotiating it is not required. It is only needed to make sure the peer sends LQRs rather than some other quality protocol, to stop the peer from keeping its own timer, or to set a maximum time between reports.

The option has Type 4, Length 8, a Quality-Protocol value of hex c025 and a four-octet Reporting-Period. That field gives the maximum time between packets in hundredths of seconds, and the peer MAY send faster. A value of zero means the peer need not keep a timer and instead sends an LQR immediately on receiving one. A zero MUST be Nak'd with a non-zero value when that peer has sent or will send its own Configure-Request with a zero period.
sections.eli5: A side can ask the other to send a report at least every so often, or to answer right away each time it gets one. Both can not ask for the answer-right-away mode at once.

sections.title: The Link-Quality-Report Packet
sections.content:
One LQR is carried in the Information field of a PPP frame whose protocol field is hex c025. Field names are relative to the receiver, since the receiver asked for the packet.

The transmitted fields are Magic-Number, LastOutLQRs, LastOutPackets, LastOutOctets, PeerInLQRs, PeerInPackets, PeerInDiscards, PeerInErrors, PeerInOctets, PeerOutLQRs, PeerOutPackets and PeerOutOctets, each four octets. The Magic-Number MUST be sent as zero and ignored unless Magic-Numbers have been negotiated, in which case it is checked to detect a looped-back link.

The LastOut... fields echo the most recently received PeerOut... values, and the PeerIn... fields echo the most recently received SaveIn... values. The PeerOut... fields are taken from the sender's own outbound counters and MUST include this LQR. Five more fields, SaveInLQRs, SaveInPackets, SaveInDiscards, SaveInErrors and SaveInOctets, are not transmitted. The receiver's Rx process logically appends them from its own inbound counters.
sections.eli5: Each report says what the sender sent, what it last heard from the other side, and what the other side said it received. Putting those side by side shows where messages went missing.

sections.title: When Reports Are Sent
sections.content:
Once LCP reaches the Opened state, link quality monitoring MAY start sending LQRs. If a Protocol-Reject names an LQR packet, it MUST stop. An LQR is usually sent when the link's LQR timer expires, and the timer MUST be restarted whenever one is sent. If no timer is used, an LQR is sent on receiving one, and negotiation ensures at least one side uses a timer.

An LQR is also generated when two successive LQRs arrive with the same PeerInLQRs value. That may mean an LQR was missed, the local side is sending much slower than the peer, or the peer sped up to measure errors better.
sections.eli5: Reports go out on a timer. If it looks like the other side is not hearing them, an extra one goes out right away.

sections.title: Calculations, Failure Detection and Policy
sections.content:
On each new LQR the Link-Manager subtracts the previous LQR's fields to get deltas. If PeerInLQRs is zero, the LastOut... fields are indeterminate and no calculations can be made yet. Counters wrap to zero at their maximum, so deltas need care.

  • LastOutLQRs against PeerInLQRs shows how many outbound LQRs were lost.
  • The change in PeerInPackets against the change in LastOutPackets shows packets lost on the outgoing link. The same comparison works for octets.
  • The change in SaveInPackets against the change in PeerOutPackets shows packets lost on the incoming link, and likewise for octets.
  • Changes in PeerInDiscards and PeerInErrors can show that loss comes from congestion at the peer rather than physical link failure.

For failure detection, the interval should be long enough to smooth the data but short enough to react to complete failure. If the link is bad outgoing, sending LQRs faster will not help. If it is bad incoming, LQRs SHOULD be sent faster. When an LQR fails to arrive or shows truly bad links, at least one additional LQR SHOULD be sent, and an algorithmic decision needs at least 2 round trip intervals.

Policy is left to the implementation, but some hysteresis is recommended so the link does not bounce. One example is a K out of N algorithm. A suggested recovery is to close all other Network-Layer protocols while still sending LQRs, then reconfigure them once quality is acceptable.
sections.eli5: Subtracting an old tally from a new one tells how many messages passed in between. If the two sides disagree, the difference is how many got lost. To avoid flip-flopping, wait for several bad checks before giving up on the wire.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC has a Security Considerations section, but it states only that security issues are not discussed in this memo. The document therefore offers no guidance on, for example, protecting the reports.
sections.eli5: The document does not say anything about keeping the reports safe from tampering.

fields.name: Reporting-Period
fields.desc: Maximum time between packets, in hundredths of seconds; zero means no timer.

items.title: Link-Manager
items.text: Sends and receives LQRs and applies the link quality policy.

items.title: Mux
items.text: Merges protocols into one stream; LQRs get the highest priority.

items.title: Tx
items.text: Counts outbound data and fills the PeerOut fields; follows Mux.

items.title: Rx
items.text: Counts inbound data and supplies the SaveIn fields.

items.title: Demux
items.text: Splits inbound packets by protocol; follows Rx.
